title: Eldorado
text:
Brightly arrayed, a gallant knight

traveled long in sun and in shadow,

singing his song, in search of Eldorado.


--


But he grew old, the spirited knight, and

night fell upon his heart because nowhere

did he find the land of Eldorado.


--


And at last, when his strength failed him, he could

find a pilgrim shadow. "Shadow," he

asked, "where might that land of

Eldorado be?"


--


"Beyond the mountains of the Moon, in

the depth of the valley of shadows; ride,

ride without rest," answered the shadow, "if

you seek Eldorado..."
editorial_note: The translation follows the Spanish catalog's prose-line form while preserving the quest refrain.

title: A Dream Within a Dream
text:
Receive this kiss upon your forehead!

And, to free myself from a burden

before departing, I confess

that you were right if you believed

that my days have been a dream;

But is it any less grave

that hope should end

by night or in full sun,

with or without a vision?

Even our last endeavor

is only a dream within a dream.


Before the roaring sea

that punishes this reef,

I hold tight in my palm

grains of golden sand.

They are few! And in a moment

they slip from me, and I feel

this lament rise in me:

Oh God! Why can I not

hold them in my fingers?

Oh God! If only I could

save one from the tide!

Is even our last endeavor

only a dream within a dream?
editorial_note: The translation keeps the Spanish version's directness and the closing question around dream, sand, and tide.

title: To Science
text:
Oh Science! You are the true daughter of

old time, you whose indiscreet gaze transforms

all things! Why do you make prey

of the poet's heart, oh vulture, whose wings are

the somber realities? How could he

love you? How could he believe you wise if you have

not wished to let him wander in his dreams in search

of treasures in the breast of the starry heavens,

though he rose there on intrepid wing?

Have you not torn Diana from her chariot,

and forced the hamadryads of the forest to seek

asylum in some other, happier star?

Have you not drawn the naiad from her wave, the elf from

his green meadow, and stolen from me myself

my summer dream beneath the tamarinds?
editorial_note: This prose-like Spanish variant of Poe's science poem is translated separately from the earlier sonnet-shaped entry.

title: Romance
text:
Oh romance, you who love to sing, your forehead

drowsy and your wings folded, among the green

leaves stirred far away over some shadowed lake,

you have been for me a brightly colored parrot,

a very familiar bird; you taught me

to read my alphabet, to babble

all my first words, while,

a child of keen gaze, I sank into sullen

woods.


--


In these later times, the eternal Condor

of time has shaken my sky so greatly,

even in its heights, enlarging the tumult

produced by the passage and flight of

the years, and I keep my eyes so stubbornly

fixed on the troubling horizon, that I have

no time left for my sweet leisure.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the catalog's Spanish rendering of Romance as a remembered bird and a later loss of leisure.

title: I Saw You on Your Bridal Day...
text:
I saw you on your bridal day, when an intense

modesty invaded your brow, though all was

joy around you and, before you,

the world was nothing but Love.


--


In the life-giving light that shone in your eyes,-whatever

its essence may have been,-I found

all that my sorrowful gaze could find

of enchantment upon the earth.


--


That modesty was perhaps nothing but virginal modesty-it could

very well pass for that,-although its splendor

made a more impetuous flame rise

still in the breast of the one who, poor man!,

saw you on your bridal day, when your brow was

covered with that unconquerable blush, although

you were surrounded by happiness and the world

was nothing but love before you!
editorial_note: The translation follows the Spanish text's long return to the bridal-day blush and the observer's sorrow.
